_meta: A series of metric samples that oscillate around an alert threshold, used to show that a single-threshold alert fires and clears on every crossing -- flapping and paging on-call repeatedly for one situation -- while a two-threshold hysteresis alert (fire high, clear low) fires once for the same sustained condition. An alert compares a metric to a threshold and fires when it crosses. The trouble is that real metrics are noisy and often sit right at the level that matters, so a value hovering near the threshold crosses up and down many times in a row. A single-threshold alert treats each up-crossing as a new incident: it fires, the metric dips below, it clears, the metric rises, it fires again, and on-call gets a page per oscillation -- alert fatigue that trains people to ignore the alert, including the real one. Hysteresis separates the fire and clear thresholds: the alert fires only when the metric exceeds a HIGH threshold and clears only when it drops below a LOWER one, so oscillations within the band between them do not toggle the alert. It fires once when the condition genuinely begins and stays fired through the noise, one page instead of many. An alternative is a 'for duration' rule that requires the breach to persist for several samples before firing; both remove the sensitivity to a single crossing. On this fixture the samples oscillate around a threshold of 80: a single threshold fires 4 times, while hysteresis with a high of 84 and a low of 76 fires once, and the samples that fall in the 76-to-84 band are exactly the ones that toggle the naive alert. The samples and the thresholds are the fixture; each alert's fire count and the in-band samples are computed. Stdlib only.
